prompt: Autocommit is on and one UPDATE over ten million rows is halfway through when the power fails. What does the table look like afterwards?
hint: Ask who opened the transaction that statement was running in.

choices.text: As it was before the UPDATE started
choices.why: A single statement is atomic on its own: autocommit wrapped it in a transaction.

choices.text: Updated as far as the last checkpoint
choices.why: Checkpoints decide what has to be replayed, and not what counts as done.

choices.text: Half updated, with no BEGIN to protect it
choices.why: The BEGIN was supplied for you, which is what autocommit means.

choices.text: Locked until somebody clears it
choices.why: Recovery finishes or undoes the work, and it needs no help to do it.

prompt: Which of these does a transaction not give you?
hint: Three of them are about when things happen, and one is about whether they are right.

choices.text: Two statements taking effect together, or neither
choices.why: That is atomicity, and it is the first thing a transaction is for.

choices.text: The ability to discard everything with ROLLBACK
choices.why: Until it commits, its work is visible to nobody and can be thrown away.

choices.text: Separation from another connection's unfinished work
choices.why: How much is a setting, and the rest of the lesson is about that setting.

choices.text: A guarantee the result makes business sense
choices.why: Constraints do that; a transaction makes two statements happen together.

prompt: In PostgreSQL a statement inside a transaction raises an error. What can you run next?
hint: There is a message about commands being ignored.

choices.text: Reads, since a SELECT changes nothing
choices.why: The block covers every statement, whether it writes or not.

choices.text: Anything: the failed statement is skipped
choices.why: MySQL behaves that way, and application code is often written against it.

choices.text: Nothing at all until you roll back
choices.why: Every later statement is refused; a SAVEPOINT beforehand is how you carry on.

choices.text: The same statement, retried by the server
choices.why: Retrying is the application's job, and it is the last section of this lesson.

prompt: Your framework offers nested transactions. What is it emitting?
hint: There is no such thing underneath.

choices.text: A savepoint inside the one transaction
choices.why: With ROLLBACK TO to undo part of the work without abandoning the whole.

choices.text: A second transaction on a second connection
choices.why: That would be a separate transaction, unable to see the first one's work.

choices.text: A queue of statements held to the outer commit
choices.why: Statements run as they are sent; holding them back would change what they read.

choices.text: A transaction whose commit is deferred
choices.why: Deferring a commit is not something the protocol offers.

prompt: A transaction has two exits: COMMIT, and ___.
hint: One of them makes the work permanent and the other makes it never have happened.

prompt: Which letter of ACID is a promise about something you did?
hint: Three are mechanisms. One depends on what you wrote down.

choices.text: D, for durability
choices.why: Hardware can undermine it, which is a different thing from you declaring it.

choices.text: I, for isolation
choices.why: You choose the level, and each level is then enforced for you.

choices.text: C, for consistency
choices.why: The database keeps the constraints you declared and has no opinion about the rest.

choices.text: A, for atomicity
choices.why: Grouping decides the scope; the guarantee inside that scope is the engine's.

prompt: An order's total should equal the sum of its lines. Does a transaction guarantee that?
hint: Ask where that rule is written down.

choices.text: Yes, at SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: That level checks for orderings, and it has no idea what your rule is.

choices.text: Yes, if both writes share a transaction
choices.why: They will happen together, whether or not the numbers agree.

choices.text: Yes, that is the C in ACID
choices.why: That letter means the rules you declared, and this one was not declared.

choices.text: No, not unless it is a constraint
choices.why: Unless it is a constraint, the rule lives in application code and nothing enforces it.

prompt: COMMIT returned, then the primary machine is destroyed. A replica that had not received the change—
hint: Durability says what it says, and it says it about one machine.

choices.text: It has it: the commit waited for the replica
choices.why: It does when configured to, and that configuration is the trade being described.

choices.text: It recovers it from the primary's log
choices.why: The primary is gone, and so is the log entry that was only there.

choices.text: It does not have it
choices.why: Synchronous replication widens the promise and costs latency on every commit.

choices.text: It is a violation of the D
choices.why: The D is about surviving a crash of the machine that committed.

prompt: You write to the database and also post to a message queue. Where does the post belong?
hint: Either order of the two lines has a failure that lies.

choices.text: Sent to the queue inside the transaction
choices.why: A message already delivered is not something a rollback can reach.

choices.text: Written to a table in the transaction
choices.why: A separate process delivers it afterwards, and the row is covered by the commit.

choices.text: Sent to the queue just after the COMMIT
choices.why: If the process dies in between, the message is never sent and nobody knows.

choices.text: Sent to the queue just before the COMMIT
choices.why: If the commit then fails, the message describes something that did not happen.

prompt: The database implements durability correctly. What can still take it away?
hint: The database can only wait for an answer; it cannot check that the answer was honest.

choices.text: An isolation level below REPEATABLE READ
choices.why: Isolation governs visibility between transactions and touches durability not at all.

choices.text: Storage that lies about flushing
choices.why: Some consumer hardware, some virtual machines, a filesystem mounted wrongly.

choices.text: A long transaction holding the log open
choices.why: That costs disk and slows recovery; the committed data is still committed.

choices.text: A crash during a checkpoint
choices.why: A checkpoint is an optimisation for recovery, and the log already has the data.

prompt: What is the useful question to ask about a database, instead of whether it is ACID?
hint: A product answers them one at a time, and so does a configuration file.

choices.text: Whether it is relational
choices.why: Several document and key-value stores now offer real transactions.

choices.text: Whether it supports two-phase commit
choices.why: A specialised protocol, and needing it is rarer than the slogan suggests.

choices.text: Which isolation level it uses by default
choices.why: A good question, and it answers one of the four rather than all of them.

choices.text: What each of the four letters means here
choices.why: What happens if this half fails, which rules are enforced, what others see, what survives.

prompt: What is a dirty read?
hint: The word points at work that has not been finished.

choices.text: Reading a value a constraint would reject
choices.why: A constraint rejects at write time, so such a value is not in the table.

choices.text: Reading a row somebody deletes next
choices.why: The row was really there when it was read, which is an ordinary race.

choices.text: Reading a row while another writes it
choices.why: Writers do not block readers, and the reader sees a committed version.

choices.text: Reading work that is not yet committed
choices.why: And then the other transaction rolls back, so the value never existed at all.

prompt: What separates a non-repeatable read from a phantom?
hint: One is about a row you had, and one is about a row you did not.

choices.text: One was committed and the other was not
choices.why: Both involve committed data; neither of them is a dirty read.

choices.text: One row changed under you, one row appeared
choices.why: A row you saw changing, against a row appearing inside a range you counted.

choices.text: One is possible at READ COMMITTED and one is not
choices.why: Both are possible there, which is what the standard's table says.

choices.text: One happens in a SELECT, one in an UPDATE
choices.why: Both are noticed by reading, which is what makes them reads.

prompt: Two connections both read a stock of 10 and both write 9. What is that called?
hint: Two sales went through and the stock moved by one.

choices.text: A phantom read
choices.why: A phantom is a row appearing in a range, and no row appeared here.

choices.text: A lost update
choices.why: Each read a true value and wrote a correct consequence of it, and one sale vanished.

choices.text: A write skew
choices.why: Write skew is two transactions writing different rows; these wrote one.

choices.text: A dirty read
choices.why: Neither saw the other at all, which is precisely the problem.

prompt: What is the first fix for a lost update?
hint: Look at where the arithmetic is being done.

choices.text: Raise the isolation level to REPEATABLE READ
choices.why: On PostgreSQL that turns it into an aborted transaction you then have to retry.

choices.text: Do the arithmetic inside the UPDATE
choices.why: stock = stock - 1 reads and writes in one statement, and the row is locked for it.

choices.text: Read the row again before writing
choices.why: The second read can be overtaken as easily as the first was.

choices.text: Put both statements in one transaction
choices.why: They probably already are, and the two transactions still do not see each other.

prompt: Why is write skew not simply a lost update?
hint: Compare which rows each transaction wrote.

choices.text: The two transactions read different rows
choices.why: They read the same rows, and that is where the shared premise comes from.

choices.text: It shows up at SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: SERIALIZABLE is the level that prevents it, rather than the one that produces it.

choices.text: The two transactions write different rows
choices.why: Nothing collided, so there is no overwrite and no conflict to detect.

choices.text: One of the two transactions is rolled back
choices.why: Both commit happily, which is what makes the pair so hard to notice.

prompt: Match each anomaly to what happens.
hint: Two of the five are not in the standard's list, and one of those is here.

pairs.right: You see work that was never committed
A row appears in a range you had already counted
Two read-modify-writes, and one overwrites the other

right_distractors: A row you read changes underneath you
Two correct decisions that are wrong together

prompt: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level?
hint: It is not the same as MySQL's, which is the point of the section.

choices.text: READ UNCOMMITTED
choices.why: PostgreSQL cannot produce a dirty read at all, so the level buys nothing.

choices.text: REPEATABLE READ
choices.why: That is MySQL's default, and running the same code on both is how people find out.

choices.text: SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: It would hand every application a retry loop it had not written.

choices.text: READ COMMITTED
choices.why: It shows no uncommitted work and it never aborts your transaction over a conflict.

prompt: The same application is deployed on PostgreSQL and on MySQL. What differs without anybody choosing it?
hint: One default against another.

choices.text: Whether a single statement is atomic
choices.why: It is on both, which is what autocommit means in each.

choices.text: Whether a deadlock is detected
choices.why: Both detect deadlocks; they differ in how quickly they look.

choices.text: Whether a transaction is atomic as a unit
choices.why: Both give atomicity, and neither makes it optional.

choices.text: The isolation level you get by default
choices.why: READ COMMITTED against REPEATABLE READ, so a bug impossible on one is routine on the other.

prompt: You ask PostgreSQL for READ UNCOMMITTED. Can you now get a dirty read?
hint: Think about what the storage keeps when a row is updated.

choices.text: No, and not at any other level
choices.why: Old versions are kept rather than overwritten, so there is no uncommitted one to read.

choices.text: Yes, that is what the level does
choices.why: The level is accepted as a spelling and behaves as READ COMMITTED.

choices.text: Yes, from another session
choices.why: Sessions are what isolation is between, so that changes nothing here.

choices.text: Yes, unless the row is locked
choices.why: A lock affects writers, and the visibility rule is decided elsewhere.

prompt: In MySQL at REPEATABLE READ, a plain SELECT reads 10 and an UPDATE then runs on the same row. What does the UPDATE read from?
hint: Locking reads and plain reads do not agree in this engine.

choices.text: The latest committed version
choices.why: So a transaction can write from a value of 12 that it never saw.

choices.text: The snapshot the SELECT saw
choices.why: That is what the level's name suggests, and it is what the writes do not do.

choices.text: Whichever version is older
choices.why: Nothing prefers the older version; the write wants the current one.

choices.text: Neither, it fails with an error
choices.why: PostgreSQL raises one there; MySQL takes a lock and proceeds.

prompt: Oracle's SERIALIZABLE permits which anomaly, despite the name?
hint: It is snapshot isolation wearing a stronger word.

choices.text: Write skew
choices.why: Two transactions reading the same rows and writing different ones are not detected.

choices.text: Dirty read
choices.why: Oracle prevents it everywhere; it has no READ UNCOMMITTED to offer.

choices.text: Phantom read
choices.why: Snapshot isolation prevents phantoms, which is more than the table requires.

choices.text: Lost update
choices.why: A conflicting write is detected and one transaction is refused.

prompt: When is REPEATABLE READ the level you actually want?
hint: The name describes the thing it is good at.

choices.text: When throughput matters more than exactness
choices.why: Raising the level costs throughput rather than buying it.

choices.text: When one transaction reads more than once
choices.why: A report of several queries, an export, a reconciliation: one view throughout.

choices.text: When a decision depends on rows others write
choices.why: That is the write-skew shape, and it needs the level above.

choices.text: When two transactions write the same row
choices.why: A conflicting write is handled at the lower level too, by waiting.

prompt: Why does snapshot isolation miss write skew?
hint: Ask what it is looking for.

choices.text: The reads were not committed
choices.why: Both read committed data, and both readings were true at the time.

choices.text: The writes touch different rows
choices.why: It detects two transactions writing the same row, and these wrote two.

choices.text: The check ran outside the transaction
choices.why: It was inside, which is what makes the example worth teaching.

choices.text: One snapshot was out of date
choices.why: Both snapshots were current and correct when they were taken.

prompt: Check that a username is free, then insert it. What shape is that?
hint: Two transactions can each find it free.

choices.text: Correct as written
choices.why: The transaction makes them happen together and stops neither of them.

choices.text: A write skew
choices.why: So the pattern is unsafe even inside a transaction; a unique index is the fix.

choices.text: A phantom read
choices.why: A phantom is the symptom here, and it does not name the bug.

choices.text: A lost update
choices.why: Nothing collides: two rows are inserted and both succeed.

prompt: Which fix works against the write skew you have not thought of yet?
hint: Two of these need you to have identified the rule first.

choices.text: FOR UPDATE on the rows you read
choices.why: It works, and you have to know which reads to protect before you protect them.

choices.text: A unique index on that column
choices.why: Excellent where the rule is uniqueness, and it has to be the rule you spotted.

choices.text: The SERIALIZABLE level
choices.why: It tracks what was read as well as written, so it catches shapes nobody enumerated.

choices.text: An exclusion constraint
choices.why: The right tool for that family, once you know the family is the problem.

prompt: Two people book the same room for half past two. What does PostgreSQL offer?
hint: It is a unique index generalised past equality.

choices.text: A CHECK on the time range
choices.why: A CHECK sees one row, and an overlap is a fact about a pair.

choices.text: A unique index on room and start time
choices.why: Two bookings that overlap without starting at the same minute slip through.

choices.text: A trigger re-running the overlap query
choices.why: It re-runs the same check that two transactions can each pass.

choices.text: An exclusion constraint using gist
choices.why: EXCLUDE USING gist: no two rows with the same room and overlapping ranges.

prompt: You choose SERIALIZABLE. What have you chosen along with it?
hint: Read the HINT on the error it produces.

choices.text: The loss of phantom protection
choices.why: It prevents phantoms as well, along with everything below it.

choices.text: A lock on each row you read
choices.why: It takes no such locks; it tracks the reads and checks them at commit.

choices.text: Writing a retry loop yourself
choices.why: The level hands you an error meaning try again, and answering it is your job.

choices.text: Longer transactions to check
choices.why: The checking is not what makes a transaction long.

prompt: In PostgreSQL, does a SELECT block an UPDATE of the same row?
hint: Ask what the storage does when a row is written.

choices.text: Yes, until the reader commits
choices.why: That is how a database without multiversion storage would have to behave.

choices.text: Yes, at REPEATABLE READ and above
choices.why: The level decides which version is read, and not whether a lock is taken.

choices.text: No, at no isolation level
choices.why: Old versions are kept, so the reader reads one while the writer writes another.

choices.text: Yes, if FOR SHARE
choices.why: FOR SHARE adds a lock; a plain SELECT takes none.

prompt: What does FOR UPDATE add to a SELECT?
hint: It is the same lock, taken earlier.

choices.text: An UPDATE's own lock
choices.why: Taken at the moment you read, so the decision you make from it holds.

choices.text: A guarantee you will not delete the row
choices.why: Your own transaction was never the risk being managed.

choices.text: A promise the value will not change
choices.why: It stops other writers for the whole transaction, not for one statement.

choices.text: A faster path to the row
choices.why: Fetching is not what the clause changes.

prompt: Ten workers pull from a jobs table with FOR UPDATE and no SKIP LOCKED. What happens?
hint: They all want the same first row.

choices.text: Each gets the row, ten times over
choices.why: The lock is exclusive, so nine of them wait rather than proceed.

choices.text: They deadlock on the one lock
choices.why: Waiting for one lock is a queue; a deadlock needs a cycle.

choices.text: They queue for one row
choices.why: So the queue processes one job at a time, whatever the worker count is.

choices.text: Each takes a different row
choices.why: Nothing hands out different rows unless the query asks to skip the locked ones.

prompt: Optimistic locking: UPDATE … WHERE id = 7 AND version = 4 affects zero rows. What does that tell you?
hint: No error was raised, so the count is the whole signal.

choices.text: The version column needs an index
choices.why: An index changes the speed and never the number of rows matched.

choices.text: The transaction needs a higher level
choices.why: The level is not what decided this; the WHERE clause is.

choices.text: The row was deleted
choices.why: A possible cause, and a rarer one than the conflict the pattern exists for.

choices.text: Somebody else saved first
choices.why: The row is at a later version, and treating zero as a conflict is the part people forget.

prompt: What is an advisory lock for?
hint: There is no row to lock.

choices.text: Locking a row before it exists
choices.why: A row that does not exist has nothing for a lock to attach to.

choices.text: Telling the planner what you will write
choices.why: The planner takes no hints from locks, and locks give it none.

choices.text: Locking something that is not a row
choices.why: One importer at a time, say: the thing being protected is a process.

choices.text: Locking a table without an ALTER
choices.why: Table-level locks exist and have their own statement.

prompt: This connection will go back to a pool. Which advisory lock do you take?
hint: One of them is released for you and one is not.

choices.text: Neither, they are unusable with a pool
choices.why: The transaction-scoped form is safe, which is why it is the one to prefer.

choices.text: The session-scoped one
choices.why: Surviving a rollback is exactly the property that makes it dangerous here.

choices.text: Either, the pool releases them
choices.why: A pool hands back a connection; it does not audit what that connection holds.

choices.text: The transaction-scoped one
choices.why: The session-scoped one is released by hand, and travels with the connection if it is not.

prompt: What is a deadlock?
hint: Draw the arrows of who is waiting for whom.

choices.text: A transaction waiting too long for a lock
choices.why: That is a lock wait timeout, and it has a different fix.

choices.text: A cycle of transactions each waiting
choices.why: Each holds what the other needs, and waiting longer resolves nothing.

choices.text: A lock not released after a commit
choices.why: Locks are released at the end of the transaction that took them.

choices.text: Two transactions writing one row at once
choices.why: One of them waits at its UPDATE, which is ordinary and fine.

prompt: PostgreSQL detects a deadlock. What happens to the data?
hint: The word in the error is detected, not corrupted.

choices.text: Both are held until somebody intervenes
choices.why: The detection exists precisely so that nobody has to step in.

choices.text: One transaction is rolled back
choices.why: Cleanly, and the other proceeds; it is neither corruption nor a crash.

choices.text: The rows stay locked until restart
choices.why: The victim's locks go with the victim's transaction.

choices.text: Both are rolled back
choices.why: Rolling back one is enough to break the cycle, so one is what goes.

prompt: Two transfers in opposite directions deadlock. What is the fix that costs nothing?
hint: The cycle needs the two transactions to disagree about an order.

choices.text: Raise the level to SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: A higher level produces more aborts here rather than fewer.

choices.text: Lock the rows in ascending order of their id
choices.why: Whichever takes row 1 also takes row 2, so the other waits and then proceeds.

choices.text: Update each account without a transaction
choices.why: That gives up the atomicity the transfer needed in the first place.

choices.text: Add a savepoint before the second update
choices.why: A savepoint marks a place to return to and takes no locks.

prompt: Two transactions take FOR SHARE on a row and then both try to update it. Why does that deadlock?
hint: Each of them needs the other to let go of something first.

choices.text: A share lock is held to the commit
choices.why: True, and it is the second half of the explanation rather than the first.

choices.text: Each waits for the other's share lock
choices.why: Take FOR UPDATE at the start, when you already know you intend to write.

choices.text: The snapshot blocks the update, not a lock
choices.why: A snapshot decides what is read; a lock decides who waits.

choices.text: FOR SHARE and UPDATE do not mix
choices.why: They do, and doing so in that order is what produces the cycle.

prompt: Deadlock detected against lock wait timeout. What is the difference?
hint: One of the two can never resolve itself.

choices.text: A rollback against a retry
choices.why: Both roll something back, and both are worth retrying once.

choices.text: Your bug against a configuration fault
choices.why: Both are usually your code, and neither is a configuration fault.

choices.text: MySQL's name against PostgreSQL's
choices.why: Both engines report both conditions, with their own numbers.

choices.text: A cycle against ordinary contention
choices.why: One needs a change of lock ordering, the other a shorter transaction.

prompt: You have made deadlocks rare by ordering your locks. What else does the application need?
hint: Rare is not the same as gone.

choices.text: To retry on a deadlock
choices.why: A new query or a batch job somebody adds is a new pair of orderings.

choices.text: A bigger lock table
choices.why: Running out of lock space is a different failure with a different message.

choices.text: A lower deadlock_timeout
choices.why: Catching them sooner spends more on checking and prevents none of them.

choices.text: To move to SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: That level adds a second reason to abort rather than removing this one.

prompt: What does one long-open transaction stop VACUUM from doing?
hint: VACUUM has to assume somebody might still be looking.

choices.text: Reclaiming the newer dead rows
choices.why: It can only reclaim versions older than the oldest running transaction.

choices.text: Reclaiming rows in the tables it touched
choices.why: The horizon is global: tables it never read are affected too.

choices.text: Running at any point
choices.why: It runs, and finds nothing it is allowed to remove.

choices.text: Refreshing the planner's statistics
choices.why: Analysing is a separate job from reclaiming, and it is unaffected.

prompt: A connection has been idle in transaction for two hours. What is it holding?
hint: The query it ran finished in a millisecond.

choices.text: A connection, and little else
choices.why: The connection is the cheapest of the things it is holding.

choices.text: A snapshot, which is free
choices.why: The snapshot is what pins the row versions, whether it is read again or not.

choices.text: Locks and old row versions
choices.why: Nobody committed, so everything the transaction took is still taken.

choices.text: A query still executing
choices.why: Its state would say active if a query were running.

prompt: Where does an HTTP call to a payment provider belong?
hint: The provider decides how long your locks are held.

choices.text: Inside, so a failure rolls it back
choices.why: A charge that has left your building is not something a rollback reaches.

choices.text: Outside the transaction entirely
choices.why: Its latency becomes the length of your transaction, and your locks wait for it.

choices.text: Inside, just before the COMMIT
choices.why: The transaction is open for the whole call wherever in it the call sits.

choices.text: Inside, wrapped in a savepoint
choices.why: A savepoint undoes database work, and the call was not database work.

prompt: You batch a ten-million-row backfill into chunks that each commit. What have you given up?
hint: The reason the batching helps is the reason something is lost.

choices.text: Little, batching is better
choices.why: The atomicity you had over the whole run is a real thing to have given up.

choices.text: Durability, one commit per batch
choices.why: Each commit is as durable as any other; committing more often loses nothing.

choices.text: Isolation, others see the batches
choices.why: They do, and that is the same visibility any committed work has.

choices.text: Atomicity over the whole job
choices.why: Half the rows are updated if it stops, so the job has to be written to resume.

prompt: What does idle_in_transaction_session_timeout do when it fires?
hint: The result is meant to be noticed.

choices.text: Writes a warning to the log
choices.why: There is a separate setting for warning, and this one acts.

choices.text: Commits what was done
choices.why: Committing work nobody asked to commit would be a far worse default.

choices.text: Rolls back but stays connected
choices.why: Leaving it connected would let the same code open another one immediately.

choices.text: Kills the session
choices.why: The application sees a dropped connection, and a bug report beats bloat.

prompt: Which SQLSTATE class means the transaction may be run again?
hint: It is the transaction rollback class.

choices.text: 23, integrity constraints
choices.why: A duplicate row is still a duplicate on the second attempt.

choices.text: 08, connection
choices.why: Reconnecting is reasonable, and it is a different kind of recovery.

choices.text: 42, syntax and access
choices.why: A query with a syntax error will have one for ever.

choices.text: 40, transaction rollback
choices.why: Nothing was written, nobody is at fault, and a second attempt may well succeed.

prompt: Why retry the whole transaction rather than the statement that failed?
hint: Think about why the first attempt was refused.

choices.text: The first statement may be repeated
choices.why: Position is not what decides it; the reads the decision rests on are.

choices.text: The failed statement is cached
choices.why: Nothing caches a statement's result between attempts.

choices.text: The decision has to be made again
choices.why: The premise it read turned out to be false, so the reads have to happen again.

choices.text: The database refuses it twice
choices.why: It accepts it happily, which is what makes the wrong version so easy to write.

prompt: Two transactions retry immediately after deadlocking. What happens?
hint: They are still in step with each other.

choices.text: They collide again
choices.why: A wait that grows, with a random component, turns a collision into a queue.

choices.text: One wins and one waits
choices.why: Both were rolled back only to start again at the same moment.

choices.text: Both succeed
choices.why: The rollback did release them, and both transactions want them again in the same order.

choices.text: The database spaces them out
choices.why: Nothing schedules retries; the retry is entirely the application's.

prompt: Attempt 1 charged a card and then hit 40001. Attempt 2 runs the same work. What has happened?
hint: Ask what the rollback was able to reach.

choices.text: The charge is rolled back along with the transaction
choices.why: A rollback undoes database writes and reaches nothing outside.

choices.text: The retry is refused, because a side effect was detected
choices.why: The database has no way to detect that anything happened outside it.

choices.text: The charge is deferred until the commit succeeds
choices.why: Deferring it would require the provider to be part of the transaction.

choices.text: The card is charged twice
choices.why: The database rolled back its own work and has no view of anything else.

prompt: Your framework has a helper that re-runs the statement that failed. Is that enough?
hint: Compare it with what the previous question decided.

choices.text: No
choices.why: The reads have to happen again too, so the loop has to go around the whole transaction.

choices.text: Yes, as long as it backs off between the attempts
choices.why: Backing off spaces out a loop that is doing the wrong thing.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the isolation level is REPEATABLE READ
choices.why: That level produces these errors rather than making the shortcut safe.

choices.text: Yes, provided the statement is the one that raised the error
choices.why: Re-running it uses the values read before the premise changed.

prompt: INSERT INTO customers VALUES ('Xico', 'xico@example.com', 'Porto') is refused by the shop. Why?
hint: Count the columns the table declares, and in what order.

choices.text: Three values given, and the table holds four
choices.why: A value left off the end would take that column's default rather than fail.

choices.text: The first value was matched to id
choices.why: No list means by position, and position one is the identity key.

choices.text: A city has to exist before it can be used
choices.why: city is plain text with nothing declared behind it.

choices.text: VALUES is not legal without the names
choices.why: It is perfectly legal without them, which is the whole trouble.

prompt: INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (3) RETURNING id, ordered_on, status. Two of those three were never sent. Where did they come from?
hint: Lesson 3 declared both of them on the table itself.

choices.text: From the row inserted just before it
choices.why: Nothing carries over between statements; each row is filled on its own.

choices.text: From the driver, which fills the gaps
choices.why: A driver sends what you gave it and invents nothing.

choices.text: From what the columns declare
choices.why: The identity supplies one and DEFAULT supplies the other.

choices.text: They arrive empty and wait for an update
choices.why: They arrive filled, which is what a default is for.

prompt: DELETE FROM customers WHERE email = 'ana@example.com' is refused, and Ana has three orders. What refused it?
hint: Read the last two words of the orders schema in lesson 1.

choices.text: The foreign key in orders, declared RESTRICT
choices.why: Exactly that, and the DETAIL line names the key still pointing at her.

choices.text: A check constraint on customers
choices.why: No check on that table looks at another one; a check cannot.

choices.text: The unique index behind email
choices.why: Uniqueness governs what goes in, and says nothing about removal.

choices.text: A trigger written by somebody
choices.why: The schema carries it, and no trigger was ever written here.

prompt: DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 3 answers DELETE 1, and order_lines held two rows for that order. What is left of those two?
hint: order_lines declares ON DELETE CASCADE on its order_id.

choices.text: Two, until a later job clears them
choices.why: Nothing later is involved; the same statement took them.

choices.text: Neither of them — the cascade followed
choices.why: The cascade removes the rows that pointed at the one you named.

choices.text: One, since a cascade goes one level
choices.why: A cascade is not counted in levels, and it took both.

choices.text: Two, and the delete ought to have failed
choices.why: Failing is RESTRICT, which is the other choice and not this one.

prompt: UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.10 runs against four rows. Which price does each row multiply?
hint: The right-hand side of a SET is evaluated per row.

choices.text: The average of the four, then shared out
choices.why: No aggregate is involved; each row is on its own.

choices.text: Its own price, as it stood beforehand
choices.why: One pass, each row computed from the value it already held.

choices.text: The first row's price, reused
choices.why: There is no first row in a set, and none is reused.

choices.text: The price it will hold once this ends
choices.why: That would be circular, and the engine reads the old value.

prompt: UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.10 is typed without its WHERE, against four rows. What is reported?
hint: Ask whether the statement is malformed or simply wrong.

choices.text: An error, because UPDATE wants a WHERE
choices.why: A WHERE is optional, and leaving it out means every row.

choices.text: A warning that names the missing clause
choices.why: Nothing warns; the statement is exactly what was asked for.

choices.text: UPDATE 4, and nothing else
choices.why: A true and complete report of what happened.

choices.text: Nothing until the transaction is closed
choices.why: The count comes back as soon as the statement finishes.

prompt: Every price went up ten per cent by accident. You correct the statement and run the right one. What is the catalogue then?
hint: Ask what the first statement left behind when the second ran.

choices.text: Right, since the second overwrote the first
choices.why: The second wrote one row; it did not revisit the other three.

choices.text: Ten per cent high, with the correction on top of it
choices.why: Two mistakes where a SELECT would have left none.

choices.text: Back at the old prices, restored by the fix
choices.why: Nothing here restores; a write does not rerun.

choices.text: Unchanged, because the first one was faulty
choices.why: The first one was valid SQL and it took effect.

prompt: What does running the same condition as a SELECT, before the UPDATE, actually buy you?
hint: It is about the condition, and not about the change.

choices.text: It warms the cache, so the write is quicker
choices.why: Any gain there is noise, and is not why anybody does it.

choices.text: It holds the rows so nobody else moves them
choices.why: A plain SELECT takes no lock that would do that.

choices.text: You see which rows the condition matches
choices.why: And you see it while the table is still untouched.

choices.text: It keeps the old values for a rollback
choices.why: A rollback needs a transaction, which is the next section.

prompt: A nightly job has to record the rows it changed, and not merely how many. What gives it those?
hint: One of these hands back the rows themselves.

choices.text: RETURNING, with the rows as they ended up
choices.why: One statement, one pass, and the rows after the change.

choices.text: The count, read back from the driver
choices.why: The count says how many and never says which.

choices.text: A SELECT afterwards on the same condition
choices.why: After the update the condition no longer matches the same rows.

choices.text: The statement log, where one is enabled
choices.why: That logs the statement and not the rows it touched.

prompt: The same job also runs on MySQL, where RETURNING does not exist at all. What does it have there?
hint: Lesson 12 is where the differences between engines live.

choices.text: A temporary table the server fills
choices.why: Nothing fills one for you; that would be yours to write.

choices.text: The same clause under another name
choices.why: MariaDB has it for two statements; MySQL has nothing of the kind.

choices.text: How many rows the statement changed
choices.why: Which is what you have, and why the count is worth reading.

choices.text: Nothing, so the job cannot be written
choices.why: It can, with a narrower record of what it did.

prompt: Somebody clicks edit on a record a colleague already has open, and watches a spinner for ninety seconds. Which clause turns that into a message?
hint: Waiting is the default, and there are two ways to refuse to.

choices.text: `NOWAIT`
choices.why: It fails at once, so the screen can say that somebody else has it open.

choices.text: `SKIP LOCKED`
choices.why: That leaves the row out silently, which on an edit screen means the record vanishes.

choices.text: `FOR SHARE`
choices.why: It waits too, and it invites a deadlock when both holders decide to write.

choices.text: `FOR KEY SHARE`
choices.why: A weaker lock still waits for whatever conflicts with it.

prompt: Two transactions each insert a child row under a different parent, in opposite orders, and they deadlock. Neither statement names a parent row. What are they contending over?
hint: Ask what has to be checked before a child row may exist.

choices.text: The index on the child table's key
choices.why: Two different children take two different entries there.

choices.text: A lock on each parent, taken to check the reference
choices.why: The parent must still be there when the child lands, so inserting one locks it.

choices.text: The sequence that generates the children's ids
choices.why: A sequence is deliberately outside the transaction and never blocks.

choices.text: The table itself, which both are writing to
choices.why: Two inserts into one table do not queue behind each other.

prompt: On MySQL, two inserts that touch no row in common deadlock anyway. What explains it?
hint: At its default level it has to stop a row appearing inside a range somebody read.

choices.text: Its detector reports a cycle that is not there
choices.why: It reports a real cycle; what is not there is a shared row.

choices.text: It locks the spaces between index entries, and those overlap
choices.why: Two keys with nothing between them can still fall in one gap.

choices.text: Its transactions escalate to a table lock above a threshold
choices.why: That is a different engine's behaviour, and it would make them queue rather than cycle.

choices.text: Inserts there take a lock on the whole index
choices.why: They take entries and gaps, not the index.

prompt: A retry loop catches every error and runs the transaction again. Which of these turns it into a loop that never ends well?
hint: Ask which failures a second attempt could not change.

choices.text: A deadlock, detected and rolled back
choices.why: Nothing was written and the other order may well work next time.

choices.text: A serialization failure under the strictest level
choices.why: That error exists in order to be retried.

choices.text: A unique violation on a row that is genuinely a duplicate
choices.why: The second attempt inserts the same row and is refused the same way, for ever.

choices.text: A lock wait that timed out once
choices.why: Worth one more attempt, and worth investigating if it repeats.

prompt: A transaction has been open for three weeks on a busy PostgreSQL system. Beyond the bloat, what does it eventually do?
hint: Something about the numbers the database gives transactions.

choices.text: It fills the write-ahead log until the disk is full
choices.why: An idle transaction writes nothing, so there is nothing accumulating there.

choices.text: It makes the database refuse new writes, to protect itself
choices.why: It holds a place in the transaction numbering, and the database stops rather than pass the wraparound.

choices.text: It is rolled back automatically after a week
choices.why: Nothing rolls it back on its own, which is why the timeout setting exists.

choices.text: It forces every index to be rebuilt on the next restart
choices.why: A restart does not rebuild indexes, and bloat survives it intact.

prompt: A transaction has been succeeding on its fourth attempt every single time, for a year, and nobody knew. What was missing from the loop?
hint: It works, so nothing errors, so nothing is written down.

choices.text: A cap on the number of attempts
choices.why: There was one, and it was never reached.

choices.text: A count of the attempts, reported somewhere
choices.why: A retry that works is invisible, and a rate is what turns it into a design problem somebody can see.

choices.text: A longer wait between attempts
choices.why: That would hide it more comfortably rather than reveal it.

choices.text: A check of the error's class before retrying
choices.why: Worth having, and it would not have said anything about a loop that succeeds.

prompt: A report that takes twenty minutes is moved to a replica so it stops bothering the main machine. What can it still hold up there?
hint: The replica is not only serving readers.

choices.text: Nothing; a replica is read-only and isolated
choices.why: It is read-only and it is not isolated from the stream it is applying.

choices.text: Its own catching up with the stream it receives
choices.why: Its replay waits for the reader, or the reader is cancelled; either way one machine reaches the other.

choices.text: The main machine's own vacuuming, always
choices.why: Only when the replica is configured to make it wait, which is a separate setting.

choices.text: Writes on the main machine, which queue behind it
choices.why: Writes there do not wait for a reader on another machine.

prompt: A ten-million-row backfill is split into batches that each commit, and it stops at batch 400. What must it have been written with, or it cannot simply be started again?
hint: Ask what the first batch would do on a second run.

choices.text: A condition that skips the rows already done
choices.why: Atomicity over the whole job was given up on purpose, so the job has to know where it got to.

choices.text: A lock held across the batches
choices.why: Holding one across all of them is the single long transaction the batching exists to avoid.

choices.text: A count of how many rows it has changed
choices.why: A number is not a position, and the rows are not in an order it can trust.

choices.text: A rollback of the batches that succeeded
choices.why: They committed, and undoing good work is not what resuming means.

prompt: Errors whose code begins with two particular digits all mean the same thing: nothing was written, nobody is at fault, and the same work may well succeed if run again. Write those two digits.
hint: It is the class the standard set aside for transaction rollbacks.

prompt: A connection whose query finished in a millisecond has held everything for two hours because nobody committed. Write the setting that kills it after a minute.
hint: Its name says the state it is watching for.

prompt: A transaction comes back with a serialization failure. Put the five steps of answering it in order.
hint: One of them is the reason the whole block has to be inside the loop.
items: Roll back, since nothing after the failure will run
Wait a short interval that grows and carries some randomness
Begin again and read everything afresh
Decide what to write from what was just read
Give up loudly once the capped number of attempts is spent
trap: The tempting shortcut is to re-run only the statement that failed, which writes a decision made from values that have since stopped being true.

prompt: Match each failure to what it asks of you.
hint: Two of them are worth a second attempt and one of them never will be.

pairs.left: A cycle in which nobody can proceed
pairs.right: Take the locks in a consistent order

pairs.left: An ordinary wait that ran out of patience
pairs.right: Shorten whatever is holding the lock

pairs.left: A row that is genuinely a duplicate
pairs.right: Do not run it again; the answer will not change

right_distractors: Raise the isolation level for that transaction
Add an index to the table being written
